issues.failure_explanation: Arbitrariness of a nonsingular diagonal S proves an infimum bound, not attainment. Already for the first-step term, take A with rows (1,0), (0,1), (1,1) and always sample all rows. Writing G=A^T S^2 A gives eta=lambda_min(G)/lambda_max(G). Its off-diagonal entry is s_3^2>0, so eta<1 for every admissible S. With S=diag(1,1,t), eta tends to 1 as t tends to zero. Thus inf(1-eta)=0, but the displayed minimum does not exist.

issues.failure_explanation: Even when scaling optimization is harmless, the coverage constraint can prevent an optimal distribution from existing. Let q=1 and use normalized rows e_1, e_2, and (e_1+e_2)/sqrt(2). Coverage requires every p_j>0, and S cancels from the bound. Here xi=min{p_2+p_3/2,p_1+p_3/2,(p_1+p_2)/2}<1/2. issues.failure_explanation: Lemma lem5 requires covariance with the quantity actually multiplied, namely the squared error norm. Nonnegative covariance with the norm does not suffice. diagnostic_evidence.quote: \item Form $B = U \Sigma V^\top$, and replace a row block of $A$ with $B$.
for both tall and wide matrices.

issues.failure_explanation: Small singular values of the replacement block need not produce small singular values of the whole matrix, especially in the tall regime. Take A formed by stacking two copies of I_2 and replace one block with q=2. The prescribed positive block singular values are 0.2 sqrt(2) and 0.2 sqrt(2)-0.01, but the modified full Gram matrix is I_2+B^T B. Its condition number is approximately 1.0026, regardless of the sampled orthogonal factors. Thus the procedure can produce an almost perfectly conditioned matrix.
